big_idea: Some events happen AT THE SAME TIME (concurrent) instead of one after another.
learning_intention: We are learning to identify and write code with concurrent events.
student_learning_goal: I can identify and write code with concurrent events.
success_criteria: I can distinguish concurrent from sequential events.
I can describe code with 2 robots moving at the same time.
I can write a 2-lane code with concurrent events.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Buzz the Bug-Buster Beetle — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Lesson 1 concurrent tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Buzz: Two robots can move AT THE SAME TIME. That's concurrent! Buzz opens: 'Read by ROW, not by LANE!'
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Buzz puppet. 'Friends — I'm Buzz the Bug-Buster Beetle. Today we learn CONCURRENT events.'

Introduce vocabulary. Write CONCURRENT and SEQUENTIAL on chart. 'Sequential = one event, then the next. Concurrent = events at the SAME TIME.'

Demonstrate. Hold up two robot markers. 'Robot 1 forward, Robot 2 turn — at the SAME MOMENT. That's concurrent. Same time-step.'

Contrast: 'Sequential — Robot 1 forward. THEN Robot 2 turn. Different time-steps.'

Real-life examples:
- Sequential: Order coffee. THEN pay. THEN receive. Three time-steps.
- Concurrent: Two skaters spinning at the same time. One time-step.
- Sequential: Tying shoes — left first, then right.
- Concurrent: Two doors opening on a car. Same time.

'Buzz code uses 2-LANE format. Top lane = Robot 1. Bottom lane = Robot 2. Each row = one time-step. Both lanes' actions in that row run TOGETHER.'

Draw on chart:
Step | Robot 1 | Robot 2
  1  |  fwd    |  fwd
  2  |  turn   |  fwd
  3  |  fwd    |  turn

'Each step is concurrent — both robots act in that step.'

'Today we identify concurrent events and start writing 2-lane code.'

steps.instruction: Whole group: identify 4 examples as concurrent or sequential. (a) 2 robots forward at same time. (b) Robot 1 then Robot 2. (c) 2 chefs cooking 2 dishes. (d) Bus arrives, then doors open.

Three stations. Station A: Sort — pair sorts 12 scenarios into concurrent or sequential. Station B: Read 2-Lane Code — pair reads existing 2-lane code and traces. Station C: Write Concurrent — pair writes their first 2-lane code.
Stretch challenge at Station C: write code where Robot 1 has 5 steps and Robot 2 has 3 steps. Which finishes first?
Discuss the time-step idea. 'Each ROW of 2-lane code is ONE time-step. Both lanes' actions in that row run simultaneously.'
steps.teacher_prompt: Demonstrate on the grid mat with both robots moving.

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the concurrent tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Ask 'Concurrent or sequential? Show me.' Mark the tracker.

steps.instruction: STRATEGY COMPARE: Two pairs share their reads of the same 2-lane code. Class debates: same time-steps? Same outcomes? Cite Bers (2019) — concurrency reading must respect simultaneity.
steps.teacher_prompt: Buzz: 'Same code, same robots — every row matters!'

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay at Station A. Use only obvious examples.
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch at Station C: 3-lane code (3 robots).
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide a structured frame: 'These events happen ___ because ___.'
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Act out concurrent vs sequential with classmates. NO-MATERIALS PATH: use floor tape or a row of two desks as the lane mat; children walk the lanes.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: distinguishes concurrent/sequential; reads 2-lane code; writes own 2-lane code.

discussion_prompts: How is it different from SEQUENTIAL?
What does each row of 2-lane code mean?
Buzz's preview: tomorrow we WRITE concurrent code (Lesson 2 — C3.1). What concurrency rule from today must hold tomorrow?
consolidation.exit_routine: Buzz's refrain — class chants: 'BUZZ says: Read by ROW, not by LANE!' (3x). Each child writes one 2-lane code segment with row labels.

assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 1 surfaces children who already grasp concurrency vs those who treat all events as sequential.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child reads 2-lane code as if each lane runs separately — repairing the lane-by-lane reading trap at Grade 3
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On 'two robots running concurrently', the dominant Grade-3 trap is parallelism-as-sequence conflation: child reads time-step-1 row as both events happening one-after-another. Bers (2019, 'Coding as Another Language') and Grover & Pea (2013, 'Computational Thinking in K-12') frame parallelism understanding as the gateway to multi-agent CT.

Today: each row = ONE time-step shared by ALL lanes. Tomorrow Lesson 2 writes concurrent code; Lesson 3 finds bugs; Lesson 4 fixes; Lesson 5 capstones.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station B. Code: Row 1: R1 fwd, R2 fwd. Row 2: R1 turn, R2 fwd. Child reads 'R1 forward, R1 turn, R2 forward, R2 forward' (lane by lane).
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'You're reading lane by lane. But concurrent code reads ROW by row. Each row is ONE time-step.'

Walk through. 'Row 1: BOTH robots forward (at the same time). Row 2: R1 turns AND R2 forward (at the same time).'

Generalise. 'Buzz reads ACROSS a row, not down a lane. Each row = one moment. Both actions happen in that moment.'

If still lane-by-lane: provide a finger trace pointer. 'Point to row 1. Read both. Point to row 2. Read both.' Force the row-wise reading.

Long-term recovery: every 2-lane reading uses 'row by row'.
expected_student_responses: (Stretched) Predicts both robots' positions after each step.
common_misconceptions: Each lane is separate. (Repair: lanes are concurrent, not sequential.)
I read top to bottom in one lane first. (Repair: read by row, not by lane.)
Concurrent means same action. (Repair: concurrent means same TIME, different actions.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child reads row-by-row but sequences within row: drill 'every cell in this ROW happens AT THE SAME TIME'; physical demo with two children stepping together.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child accepts simultaneity but loses lane-track: two-finger pointing — index on left lane, middle on right; child moves both fingers down the rows together.
DIAGNOSTIC C — child handles 2 lanes but breaks at 3+: drop to 2 lanes only; build up after fluency.

parts_outline.task: Sort 8 scenarios as CONCURRENT or SEQUENTIAL.
Write 1 of your own 2-lane code with 4 time-steps.
